# The problem

TorNet^[Veillette et al., "TorNet: A Benchmark Dataset for Tornado Detection and Prediction
Using Full-Resolution Polarimetric Weather Radar Data," *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth
Systems*, 2024, <https://doi.org/10.1175/AIES-D-24-0006.1>. Code at
<https://github.com/mit-ll/tornet>, weights at
<https://huggingface.co/tornet-ml/tornado_detector_baseline_v1>.] is a tornado detection
benchmark: storm-centered radar chips labeled for whether a tornado is in them, and a
published CNN that looks at one scan and answers that question. Detection isn't what's missing
in the last few minutes before a touchdown, though. What would help is a signal that shows up
before the signature is obvious on the display. So the question here is a prediction one.
Every TorNet sample has four consecutive scans of a storm about five minutes apart, each with
its own label. We give a model the two oldest and ask how likely a tornado is in each of the
two newest: roughly five and ten minutes after the last thing it saw.

The framing has to be protected from detection, because a tornado already on the radar is
trivial to carry forward. So we only score on *pre-onset* cases: tornado samples where neither
input scan is tornadic and the last target scan is. A tornado visible in an input scan makes
the sample *ongoing*, reported separately and left out of the positives. Every non-tornadic
sample stays in as a negative, and the headline negatives are the hard ones, same as the TorNet
paper: storms under a tornado warning that never produced one. Telling a tornadic storm from
clear air is easy; telling it from a warned storm that looked a lot like it is the job.

Two reference points turn an AUC into a result, and both come from the published detector,
frozen, as released. Run it on the newest observed scan and score against the future labels:
that's the *floor*, what a forecaster effectively already has. Run it on the real future scan:
that's the *ceiling*, what detection would give if the forecast of the radar were perfect. A
model lands somewhere between, and what we report is its paired bootstrap difference from the
floor on the same files, with a 95% interval.

# The data

TorNet v1.1 is 203,133 samples from 2013 to 2022, CC BY 4.0, split by the authors into train
and test: 13,857 confirmed tornadoes, 64,510 warned storms, 124,766 random storms. A sample is
four NEXRAD dual-pol scans on a storm-centered polar grid, 120 azimuths by 240 range gates at
two tilts, six products plus a range-folding mask, with a label per scan. We repackaged it on
the Hugging Face Hub^[<https://huggingface.co/datasets/jakeryderv/tornet>: every field as
Parquet, one config per year, lossless and verified against the original files.] so a year is
a config and a training set is a list of years, and published the detector's weights as a
PyTorch state dict next to it^[<https://huggingface.co/jakeryderv/tornet-detector-torch>,
checked against the Keras original's logits to 2×10^-5^.].

Everything below is 2014 and 2015. Both of us worked from the same two years but cut them
differently, because we were asking different questions of them. For the detection-task steps
(1 and 2 below) the data is a 6,414-clip subset split by storm group, so episodes that share
radar dates stay together and clips near the detector's own training data are excluded: 3,667
train, 1,325 validation, 1,422 test with 89 positives. For the onset steps (3 and 4) it is the
authors' full partitions: 37,168 training samples with 15% of days held out for validation,
and the 6,448-sample test set with its 495 pre-onset cases, 208 of which are already tornadic
at five minutes and all of which are at ten.

Every model sees a scan exactly as the published detector does: the detector's normalization,
fourteen channels with the range-folding masks, and its two coordinate channels. Keeping that
representation is what lets the published weights drop in with no adapter.

# The models

Both models start from the published detector's CNN: four blocks of CoordConv 3×3 layers with
48, 96, 192 and 384 filters, each followed by 2×2 max pooling and dropout, ending in a
384-channel map over an 8 × 15 grid of cells, 4.67M parameters.

**Frozen features, small head.** For the detection steps the CNN stays frozen and each scan is
reduced to its 384 spatially pooled features, scaled, and read by a 385-parameter linear head
that predicts tornado presence in the current scan. With two scans, the current and the one
five minutes earlier, the two vectors are averaged before the head. Three seeds, thirty epochs;
validation picks the epoch and an operating threshold at 80% recall, and the test set is
touched once after that choice is locked.

**Two scans, the authors' head, onset target.** For the onset steps the CNN runs on both input
scans with shared weights and the two 384-channel maps are concatenated cell by cell. On top
sits a fresh copy of the authors' own head: two 1×1 convs of 512 and 256 channels, a 1×1 conv
to one logit per cell per horizon, and the max over cells, so the map before the max says where
the model thinks the tornado will be. One loss, weighted binary cross-entropy of each horizon's
logit against that future scan's label with the authors' sample weights; AdamW, cosine
schedule, mixed precision, early stopping on validation AUC with a cap of five epochs. The head
is always new since its job changed; the encoder is frozen in step 3 and unfrozen at a tenth of
the head's learning rate in step 4.

# The ladder

The work is five steps that each change one thing. The first two stay on the task the detector
was built for, to check the ingredients before the task changes.

| step | what changes | the question |
|:--:|:--|:--|
| 0 | Nothing trained. The published detector as designed, one scan. | What does it already give? On the onset task, the newest observed scan is the floor and the real future scan the ceiling. |
| 1 | A new linear head on the frozen features, current scan, detection target. | Can a retrained head beat the detector at its own job? |
| 2 | The scan five minutes earlier added, features averaged. | Does a second scan carry anything the first doesn't? |
| 3 | Frozen CNN, both scans concatenated, the authors' head retrained on the +5 and +10 labels. | Can the detector's own features be re-aimed at "will it appear"? |
| 4 | The CNN unfrozen at a tenth of the head's learning rate. | Does adapting the features to the target buy more? |

: The five steps. {#tbl-ladder}

Steps 1 and 2 are scored by average precision on the storm-grouped test set; steps 0, 3 and 4
by pre-onset AUC on the authors' test partition. They don't share a number: the first pair
establishes two assumptions the second pair leans on.

# Results

## Steps 1 and 2: frozen features on the detection task

| configuration | validation AP (3 seeds) | test AP | at the locked threshold |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--|
| original pretrained CNN | | 0.517 | 68 of 89 found, 276 false alarms |
| step 1: current scan, linear head | 0.658 ± 0.005 | 0.508 | 70 found, 571 false alarms |
| step 2: two-scan mean, linear head | 0.675 ± 0.001 | 0.548 | 69 found, 564 false alarms |
| current scan, MLP head (24,705 params) | 0.670 ± 0.007 | | not selected |
| warned negatives weighted ×2 | 0.656 ± 0.005 | | not selected |

: Detection target, 2014–2015 storm-grouped split. Validation chose step 2; the test set was
scored once afterwards. {#tbl-detection}

Step 1 answers its question with a no. A linear head on the frozen features lands at 0.508 test
AP against the original detector's 0.517, and neither head capacity nor reweighting moved
validation: an MLP with sixty times the parameters reached 0.670 and hard-negative reweighting
0.656, both inside seed noise of the linear 0.658. The detector's own head is about as good as
its features allow, so anything more has to come from new information, not a better readout.

Step 2 answers yes, with a caveat. Averaging in the scan from five minutes earlier was the only
change that moved validation, 0.658 to 0.675 at the same 385 parameters, and it carried to the
test set at 0.548. But better ranking did not mean fewer false alarms: at thresholds locked for
the same recall it found one more tornado than the original detector and raised 288 more false
alarms, and the paired storm-group bootstrap on its AP gain, [−0.061, +0.155], includes zero.
Ten test storm groups and 89 positives can't do better. What it does establish is that the
second scan carries signal the first doesn't, which is what steps 3 and 4 lean on.

![Step 1 and 2 configurations on validation (left) and the held-out test precision-recall
curves with locked operating points (right).](figures/jg_adaptations_pr.png){#fig-detection width=85%}

## Steps 0, 3 and 4: the onset task

| step | +5 min | paired vs floor | +10 min | paired vs floor |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 0, floor: detector on the newest scan | 0.731 [0.697, 0.767] | | 0.726 [0.701, 0.750] | |
| 0, ceiling: detector on the future scan | 0.769 [0.734, 0.806] | +0.038 [+0.016, +0.063] | 0.797 [0.772, 0.822] | +0.071 [+0.048, +0.093] |
| 3, frozen CNN, two scans, new head | 0.699 [0.662, 0.737] | −0.032 [−0.045, −0.020] | 0.710 [0.683, 0.736] | −0.017 [−0.024, −0.010] |
| 4, fine-tuned CNN, two scans, new head | 0.724 [0.689, 0.762] | −0.007 [−0.031, +0.015] | 0.728 [0.701, 0.752] | +0.001 [−0.016, +0.018] |

: Pre-onset WC AUC on the 2014–2015 test partition, 95% bootstrap intervals; the paired column
is the difference from the floor on the same files. {#tbl-onset}

Step 0 sets the stakes. The detector carried forward from the newest scan already separates
pre-onset tornadic storms from warned nulls at 0.73, so the signature is often half-formed five
minutes before the label flips. The ceiling is only 0.04 higher at +5 and 0.07 at +10: even a
perfect picture of the next scan, read by this detector, adds that much and no more, and
anything steps 3 and 4 gain has to fit inside it.

![Each step's AUC with its 95% interval, between the floor and the ceiling, per
horizon.](figures/ladder.png){#fig-ladder width=62%}

Step 3 lands below the floor, and not by noise: −0.032 at +5 and −0.017 at +10, both
intervals clear of zero. A fresh head on the frozen features, even with two scans to difference,
does not match the published head simply carried forward. That is step 1's answer again on the
harder task: the detector's own readout of its features is as good as those features get.

Step 4 recovers the floor and no more. Letting the CNN adapt lifts the head by 0.025 at +5 and
0.018 at +10 over the frozen version, to a tie with the detector at both horizons, with paired
intervals centered on zero. Validation was still rising when the five-epoch cap hit
(@fig-training), while the frozen head peaked at epoch two, so a longer fine-tune might take a
little more; the ceiling bounds what "more" can be at 0.045 and 0.07. Per year it's the same
picture with the usual noise: the fine-tuned head ties the floor in 2015 and trails it in 2014.

Put together, the ladder says that for the ten minutes before onset, two scans read by this CNN
carry about what the latest scan already carries. The second scan's gain from step 2 is real on
the detection task and does not survive the move to "will it appear". The honest summary of a
forecaster built this way is that it reproduces the detector carried forward, which is the
tool a forecaster already has.

![Validation AUC and loss per epoch for steps 3 and 4; the star marks the checkpoint
kept.](figures/training.png){#fig-training width=62%}

# What's next

The ceiling says where the rest of the signal isn't. Even a perfect radar forecast adds at most
0.07 here, and two scans didn't find any of it, so the gains have to come from information that
isn't in the chip, like the near-storm environment, and from longer histories than two scans,
where a recurrent model would finally have something to recur over. Both are config changes away with the data on the Hub by
year. The practical fix we'd make first is to the data itself: the shards store arrays as
nested lists, and decoding them is where every run spends its time.
